questions.question: Has any solid fuel been tested above 30% oxygen?

answer.text: No. The highest oxygen level in any solid-fuel data table in PSI is 22.2%, in BASS-II.
Of the 270 runs at 30% oxygen or more, all come from gas flames (ACME Flame Design, ACME CFI-G) or fuel droplets (FLEX).
The closest evidence for materials is ACME BRE, a gas burner that emulates burning solids: its flames kept burning without airflow in elevated-oxygen atmospheres but went out at 21% oxygen.

questions.question: Does shutting off ventilation put a fire out in microgravity?

answer.text: Not reliably. ACME BRE saw flames emulating PMMA and Nylon keep burning steadily with no airflow, even though stopping ventilation is an established step in fighting spacecraft fires.
That held in elevated-oxygen atmospheres; at 21% oxygen the same flames went out in a short time.
BASS also found that a local suppressant jet pulled in air and kept a flame burning even with the ambient airflow turned off.

questions.question: Is NASA's normal-gravity flammability test conservative for space?

answer.text: Not always. NASA states that the 1-g screening test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) is not conservative, because materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.

SAFFIRE-II, the one study with matched burns in both gravities, shows it depends on the material: silicone and PMMA burned less in microgravity, while the cotton-fiberglass fabric burned its full length in both.

questions.question: Which data supports a lunar habitat at 30% oxygen and 70.3 kPa?

answer.text: Very little. Of 875 runs with both oxygen and pressure, 23 fall within 5 oxygen points and 10 kPa of this atmosphere, all of them FLEX fuel droplets.
No solid-fuel table records pressure, and the highest solid-fuel oxygen is 22.2%, 7.8 points short.
None of the 19 flight investigations ran at lunar gravity.

questions.question: What evidence exists for NASA's Exploration Atmosphere (34% oxygen, 56.5 kPa)?

answer.text: Only 19 runs fall within 5 oxygen points and 10 kPa of it, all ACME CFI-G gas flames.
FLEX-2, CFI and ACME CFI-G recorded pressure ranges that include 56.5 kPa; none of them burned solid fuels.
The highest solid-fuel oxygen tested is 11.8 points below this atmosphere.

questions.question: Is there any evidence at Moon or Mars gravity?

answer.text: No. All 19 flight investigations ran in microgravity, so there is no partial-gravity evidence in this collection.
The one gravity comparison available is SAFFIRE-II, which lists normal-gravity burn lengths next to its microgravity results.

questions.question: Would an Earth smoke detector work on a spacecraft?

answer.text: NASA says probably not as designed: smoke particles from microgravity fires differ greatly in size, so a terrestrial detector would be looking for the wrong signature.
SAME and SAME-R measured smoke from overheated spacecraft materials in the station glovebox to provide that microgravity baseline.
The first SAME flight's particle samples came back contaminated and unusable, one reason SAME-R reflew.

questions.question: Do gaseous suppressants work as well in space as on Earth?

answer.text: FLEX found the flammability limit is lower in microgravity, so inert-gas suppressant standards set on Earth give less margin of safety in space.
For heptane and methanol droplets, the limiting oxygen index was significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than predicted.
For burning solids, BASS found that nitrogen applied to a flame could make it stronger by drawing in oxygen.

questions.question: What airflow is most dangerous for burning materials in microgravity?

answer.text: NASA states that for flame spread over solids, the lowest oxygen that supports burning occurs near 10 cm/s, the typical speed of spacecraft ventilation, where spread rate is also highest.
Direction matters too: in SAFFIRE-I at 20 cm/s, the flame spreading with the flow burned for 420 s, against the flow for 70 s.

questions.question: Do flames spread differently in microgravity?

answer.text: Yes. At low airflow in space, a thin fuel lit in the middle spreads its flame upstream into the oncoming air, the opposite of normal gravity.
BASS, BASS-II and the Saffire flights burned solids in both opposed and concurrent flow.

questions.question: What are cool flames and why do they matter for fire safety?

answer.text: FLEX saw that after the visible flame around a heptane droplet went out, a stable low-temperature cool flame formed and kept burning.
NASA notes the cool flame can burn for a prolonged time, a result many researchers had thought impossible.
A fire that looks extinguished may therefore still be reacting; CFI and ACME CFI-G study cool flames in more detail.
None. No solid-fuel table in PSI records pressure, so FlameMap assumes cabin pressure for them and labels it as assumed.
The lowest recorded pressure in any table is 50.7 kPa, in FLEX-2 fuel-droplet tests.

questions.question: Is there any data near a spacesuit atmosphere?

answer.text: No. Of 875 runs with both oxygen and pressure, none is within 5 oxygen points and 10 kPa of 100% oxygen at 29.6 kPa.
The highest oxygen in any table is 40%, in gas flames, and no recorded pressure range includes 29.6 kPa.

questions.question: Which materials were burned in both microgravity and normal gravity?

answer.text: Only SAFFIRE-II lists both. None of its four silicone samples burned in microgravity, though two burned completely in 1-g.
Both PMMA samples burned completely in 1-g but only about 10 cm in microgravity, and the cotton-fiberglass fabric burned its full 29 cm in both.

questions.question: Which studies reached the highest oxygen levels?

answer.text: Gas-flame studies: ACME BRE, ACME Flame Design and ACME CFI-G all reached 40% oxygen.

Flame Design and CFI-G were not aimed at fire safety, but they are the only runs near the oxygen levels proposed for future habitats; 37 runs reached 30% oxygen or more at 75 kPa or less, from ACME CFI-G and FLEX.

questions.question: Do flames make smoke differently in low gravity?

answer.text: Yes. NASA states that gas-jet flames start producing smoke at substantially different conditions in low gravity than on Earth, contrary to earlier predictions.
SPICE measured the smoke point of gas-jet flames on the station, and SLICE reused its hardware.
